opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real tension here. A lot of my work, like GPQA and more recently the time-horizon work at METR, has pushed toward tasks that are more realistic, and I do think realism matters a lot if what you ultimately care about is "what happens when these systems get deployed in the world." But I don't want to dismiss the constrained stuff, because I think it's valuable in a few distinct ways.

The first is just measurement precision. When you make a task really clean and well-specified, with an unambiguous answer and an automatic scoring function, you get a much less noisy signal. Realistic tasks are messy: there are a dozen ways to succeed, a dozen ways to partially succeed, and grading them often requires human judgment or a lot of careful rubric design. With constrained tasks you can run thousands of samples cheaply and actually see trends clearly. If you want to detect that capabilities are changing, and how fast, that precision is really useful.

The second is that constrained tasks let you isolate specific abilities. If a model fails at a big realistic software engineering task, it's often hard to say why. Was it planning? Was it some specific knowledge gap? Did it lose track of context? Did it just not check its work? A narrow task that targets one of those components can tell you something the holistic task can't. It's kind of like the difference between a field study and a controlled experiment. You lose ecological validity, but you gain the ability to make causal-ish claims about what's going on.

The third, which I think people underrate, is that they can work as early-warning indicators. Often a capability shows up first in a stripped-down setting before models can reliably deploy it in messy real-world conditions. So if you're doing something like dangerous-capability evaluation, it's useful to know "the model can do the core reasoning step here, even if it can't yet string it all together." That tells you the gap might be closing.

That said, I think the big risk is over-interpreting them. There's a pretty consistent pattern where models look superhuman on a clean benchmark and then are surprisingly brittle on the messier version of the same thing. Constrained tasks tend to strip out exactly the stuff that's hard in practice: ambiguity, figuring out what the actual goal is, dealing with environments that aren't set up nicely for you, long chains of dependent actions where errors compound. So you can't just extrapolate from "aces the toy task" to "can do the job." I think the healthiest approach is to have a portfolio: constrained tasks for precision and diagnosis, realistic tasks to keep you honest about what the numbers actually mean, and ideally some way of relating the two so you can tell when the constrained results are or aren't predictive.

r001.rationale: The response says constrained tasks can isolate specific abilities and reveal whether a model can perform a core reasoning step, using them to diagnose capabilities and flag emerging ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a bunch of value there, and it's maybe a little counterintuitive because the obvious objection is, well, if the task isn't realistic, why do we care how models do on it?

The way I think about it is that there are really two different questions you might be asking with an evaluation. One is "can this model do the job?" where the job is some real thing people actually want done, and for that you obviously want realism. But the other question is more like, "what is this model fundamentally capable of?" in terms of some narrower underlying ability, reasoning or long-horizon planning or whatever it is. And for that second question, realism can actually get in the way, because realistic tasks are messy. They bundle together a ton of different skills, and when a model fails, it's really hard to tell why. Was it the reasoning? Was it that it couldn't find the right file? Was it tool use? Was it that the task was underspecified and it guessed wrong about what you wanted?

So with a very constrained task, you can kind of isolate the thing you care about. You strip away all the stuff that isn't the variable you're trying to measure. It's sort of like a controlled experiment versus a field study. The field study tells you what happens in practice, the controlled experiment tells you about mechanisms.

The other thing constrained tasks give you is that you can make them very hard in a precise way, and you can make them actually gradeable. If I give a model a task that is "do a week of research," I have a really hard time scoring that reliably. But if the task is extremely well-specified, there's a ground truth, and I can run it a thousand times and get a clean signal. That matters a lot when you're trying to track capabilities over time or compare models, because the noise in realistic evals can swamp the thing you're actually trying to see.

And then there's a more forecasting-oriented angle, which is that if a model can't do the constrained version of something, that's pretty strong evidence it can't do the realistic version either, because the realistic version is usually strictly harder. So they work as a sort of lower bound or a leading indicator. The converse isn't true, of course. Succeeding on the toy version doesn't tell you much about the real version, and I think people get tripped up on that direction a lot.

So I'd say the value is real, but you have to be honest about what claim you're licensed to make. Constrained tasks are great for understanding, for diagnosis, and for ruling things out. They're bad at telling you what a model will actually do when you deploy it. And I think a lot of the confusion in the field comes from people using one kind of eval to answer the other kind of question.

r001.rationale: The response says constrained tasks help isolate and diagnose underlying abilities, and that failure on them provides evidence the model cannot do the harder realistic task—using them to bound capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the main value is that they let you isolate a particular capability. If you look at a model doing some complicated, realistic task, there are lots of reasons it might fail. It might not understand what you’re asking, it might lack some relevant knowledge, or it might have trouble putting together a long sequence of steps. In a constrained setting, you can control some of those things and get a clearer sense of what’s actually difficult for it.

The caveat is that you have to be careful about what you infer. Success on a very simplified task doesn’t necessarily mean the model can do the corresponding thing in the real world. But if you think some capability is necessary for a more realistic task, and the model can’t demonstrate it even in a setting where you’ve removed a lot of the other difficulties, that’s useful evidence. So I see these tasks as a way of testing specific hypotheses about capabilities, rather than as a complete measure of how useful or capable a model is.

r001.rationale: It says constrained tasks isolate specific capabilities and provide useful evidence about what a model can or cannot do, while cautioning that they are not a complete measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is that they let you isolate what’s going on. With a realistic task, if a model fails, there are often lots of possible explanations. It might lack some relevant knowledge, misunderstand the instructions, or struggle with one particular step. A constrained task can help you distinguish between those explanations.

Of course, that also limits what you can conclude. If a model succeeds at a very artificial task, that doesn’t automatically mean it can handle the corresponding real-world problem. But if you’re trying to understand a particular capability, having a setting where you can vary one thing at a time and see what changes can be quite useful. I’d see those tasks as complementary to more realistic evaluations.

r001.rationale: It says constrained tasks help isolate causes of failure and distinguish explanations, and can help understand a particular capability—communicating their diagnostic value for assessing capability.
